lines.cap: **Narrator:** Banyan Hill International School, Singapore. Year 8. Tuesday, Period 3.
**Narrator:** This documentary is about how children learn English. That was the plan.
**Mr H:** Right, 8H. This term: **Shakespeare**.
**Mei:** Sir, he's four hundred years old, it's boring, and nobody talks like that.
**Narrator:** This is Mei. She is twelve. She reviews everything.
**Mei:** Canteen curry puff: four stars. Shakespeare: **one star**.
**Narrator:** Four p.m. The school library.
**Will:** ONE. STAR?
**Mei:** Who said that?
**Will:** I am **William Shakespeare**. I wrote Romeo and Juliet. I wrote Hamlet. I have never had ONE STAR.
**Mei:** You're a ghost.
**Will:** I am a ghost with feelings.
**Narrator:** Will has haunted this library since it got air-conditioning.
**Will:** I came to Singapore for the theatre. I stayed for the aircon.
**Will:** Give me one week, child. By Friday, thou shalt give me **five stars**.
**Mei:** Did you just call me **thou**?
**Will:** We'll get to that.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode one: One Star.
**Narrator:** Wednesday. Will begins, as all great men do, by talking about himself.
**Will:** Born in **Stratford-upon-Avon**, in **1564**. Son of a glove-maker.
**Mei:** Gloves. Cool. Moving on.
**Will:** Married **Anne Hathaway** at eighteen. Three children. Then, for seven years, there are almost no records of me.
**Narrator:** Historians call them the **lost years**.
**Will:** I call them none of your business.
**Will:** By **1592** I was writing plays in **London**. A jealous rival called me an 'upstart crow'. I have not forgotten.
**Nib:** Nib. Fountain pen. Technical terms. Every company of actors needed a **patron**: a powerful noble or monarch to protect it.
**Will:** We were the **Lord Chamberlain's Men**. Then **Elizabeth I** died, **James I** took us on, and we became the **King's Men**.
**Nib:** And every play was licensed by a censor, the **Master of the Revels**.
**Will:** He cut my best bits. One star.
**Will:** I died in **1616**. Seven years later, my friends printed **36** of my plays in the **First Folio**. Without it, Macbeth and The Tempest might be lost.
**Mei:** Okay. So what kinds of plays?
**Nib:** **Comedy**: confusion and disguise, ending in harmony, usually a **marriage**.
**Nib:** **Tragedy**: a high-status hero with a **fatal flaw**, called **hamartia**, which destroys them.
**Nib:** **History**: English kings. **Romance**: late plays like The Tempest, ending in **forgiveness** and **reunion**.
**Mei:** So comedy doesn't mean funny. It means the mess gets sorted out. Like my bedroom. Eventually.
**Mei:** Still one star.
**Will:** Come, child. Fifteen ninety-nine. My Globe.
**Narrator:** The **Globe**: an open-air playhouse on **Bankside**, on the south bank of the River Thames.
**Will:** Round. Wooden. Open to the sky. I called a theatre '**this wooden O**'.
**Narrator:** Around **3,000** people could squeeze in. A flag on the roof meant: a play today.
**Narrator:** In the **yard** stood the **groundlings**. They paid **one penny** to stand.
**Mei:** A penny to stand for three hours? That's the MRT at rush hour, but with murders.
**Will:** The **galleries** cost two pennies. Three, for a cushion.
**Nib:** The **thrust stage** pushes out into the yard: the audience surrounds the actors on **three sides**. Perfect for whispering secrets to the crowd.
**Narrator:** The groundlings ate, drank, wandered about and heckled. Mostly Will.
**Mei:** Where are the lights?
**Will:** There are none. We played in the afternoon, in **daylight**, with almost no scenery. If it's night, the actors must SAY so.
**Nib:** Critics call it **word scenery**: the language paints the time, the place and the mood.
**Mei:** And who's playing Juliet?
**Will:** Robert. He's thirteen.
**Narrator:** Women could not act on the English public stage until **1660**. Every female role was played by a **boy actor**.
**Narrator:** In **1613**, a cannon fired during a play set the thatched roof alight. The Globe burned down.
**Mei:** Was that a review?
**Will:** It was a SPECIAL. EFFECT.
**Mei:** Okay. Two stars. The fire was cool.
**Narrator:** Thursday, Period 1. Mr Hargreaves has had one cup of tea. He needs four.
**Mr H:** Shakespeare writes in three modes. Mode one: **blank verse**.
**Nib:** Blank verse is **unrhymed iambic pentameter**.
**Mr H:** Unrhymed. For **noble** characters, **serious** matters, **love** and **strong emotion**.
**Mr H:** On the page, every line of verse starts with a **capital letter** and stops before the margin.
**Mr H:** Mode two: **prose**. Ordinary sentences, **no fixed rhythm**, running right across the page.
**Nib:** Prose is for **servants**, **comedy**, **letters**... and **madness**.
**Nib:** Lady Macbeth sleepwalks in prose. Her controlled mind has collapsed.
**Mei:** So posh people speak verse, servants speak prose. Easy.
**Will:** Ah. A **rule of thumb**. Not a rule.
**Will:** In The Tempest, **Caliban**, a servant they call a monster, speaks some of the most beautiful verse in the play.
**Will:** And the drunken butler, Stephano, answers him in **prose**. Who is the real monster, hmm?
**Mr H:** So when a character **switches**, ask: why here, and why now? That's where the marks are.
**Mr H:** Mode three: **rhyming couplets**. Two lines in a row that rhyme. With no curtain, they **end a scene** with a click.
**Will:** The play's the thing, wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king!
**Mr H:** Couplets also mark the **supernatural**, like spells, and **lovers in harmony**.
**Mei:** He bowed. At his own couplet.
**Will:** It deserved a bow.
**Narrator:** Lunch. Mei is counting syllables on her fingers. She has run out of fingers.
**Mr H:** Break it down. An **iamb** is two syllables: **unstressed**, then **stressed**. da-DUM.
**Nib:** **Penta** means five, as in pentagon. **Five** iambs in a line. So, **ten syllables**.
**Will:** But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?
**Mr H:** Ten syllables, five stresses, landing on the key words: **soft**, **light**, **window**, **breaks**.
**Mei:** Like the memory trick: i-AM, i-AM, i-AM, i-AM, i-AM.
**Mei:** Wait. Today I want to eat some kaya toast.
**Will:** That... is iambic pentameter.
**Mei:** So I'm basically Shakespeare.
**Will:** You are basically hungry.
**Will:** Now. Listen for when the heartbeat **skips**.
**Will:** To be, or not to be, that is the question.
**Mr H:** **Eleven** syllables. The extra unstressed one at the end is a **feminine ending**.
**Nib:** The line **trails away**, unresolved. Like Hamlet's mind.
**Kevin:** Sorry. Hi. Kevin. Comma. That's me, after 'to be'.
**Kevin:** A strong pause in the **middle** of a line is a **caesura**. That's me! Today. Usually I'm in the wrong place.
**Mr H:** **Trochaic inversion** flips the first foot: DUM-da. 'Now is the winter of our discontent.' It hits the first word hard.
**Will:** And my witches don't use pentameter at all. Double, double, toil and trouble. **Trochees**. Four beats. A **spell**.
**Mr H:** Never just write 'this is iambic pentameter'. Say what the rhythm **does**, at that moment.
**Mei:** Three stars. For the kaya toast.
**Narrator:** Seven p.m. Mei's flat in Queenstown. Will has followed her home.
**Mei:** You can't be here. My Ah Ma is in the kitchen.
**Will:** Then I shall be quiet.
**Narrator:** He was not quiet.
**Will:** First: I wrote in **Early Modern English**. Not Old English. That's Beowulf.
**Mei:** So what's **thou**? You called me thou. Is that the posh one?
**Will:** The opposite! **Thou** is **familiar**: for friends, family, lovers, children, servants... or **insults**.
**Nib:** **You** is **polite** and **formal**: for superiors, strangers, or more than one person.
**Mei:** Ah Ma, thou art the best cook in Queenstown!
**Ah Ma:** Did you just thou me? I was reading Shakespeare before your mother was born. To your grandmother, you say **you**.
**Will:** I like her.
**Nib:** **Thou, thee, thy, thine** work like **I, me, my, mine**. Thou **art**. Thou **hast**. He **hath**.
**Will:** A **switch** is a **signal**. The Queen tells her son: Hamlet, thou hast thy father much offended.
**Will:** He throws it back: Mother, you have my father much offended.
**Nib:** Her warm, parental **thou**. His cold, formal **you**. A whole argument in two pronouns.
**Will:** Now. The most famous mistake in English. O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?
**Mei:** Where are you, Romeo?
**Nib:** **Wherefore** means **WHY**. **Why** must he be Romeo: a Montague, her family's enemy?
**Will:** And I invented **lonely**, **eyeball** and **swagger**.
**Nib:** You're the **earliest recorded user**, Will. Some were probably already being spoken.
**Will:** Same thing.
**Nib:** It is not the same thing.
**Mei:** So he's not the first person to say it. He's the first person whose post survived.
**Narrator:** Friday. The school hall. Will has volunteered to help Drama Club. Nobody asked.
**Nib:** **Dramatic devices**: techniques that only work in a play, because they depend on the **audience**.
**Mr H:** A **soliloquy**: a character who believes they're **alone on stage** speaks their private thoughts aloud.
**Will:** Like Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be'. Alone. Honest. We become his confidant.
**Mei:** Wait. So when I talk to the camera, on my own...
**Will:** That's a soliloquy. With worse lighting.
**Mr H:** An **aside** is **short**. Spoken to the audience, and the other characters on stage **don't hear it**.
**Will:** Hamlet's very first line is an aside about his uncle: A little more than kin, and less than kind!
**Mei:** Mr H has had five cups of tea today.
**Mr H:** I heard that.
**Mei:** You're not supposed to hear an aside!
**Mr H:** A **monologue** is a long speech to **other characters**, who are **listening**. 'All the world's a stage' is a monologue, **not** a soliloquy.
**Narrator:** **Dramatic irony**: the **audience knows** something a character **doesn't**.
**Nib:** Romeo thinks Juliet is dead. We know she has only taken a **sleeping potion**.
**Mei:** Romeo, NO! She's ASLEEP!
**Will:** I even told you the ending in the Prologue: a pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life.
**Nib:** **Foreshadowing**. Now we watch **how** it happens, not **what**. Every happy moment hurts.
**Nib:** Eight devices to know: **S**ome **A**ctors **M**umble; **S**ome **D**irectors **F**ear **P**un **C**ontests.
**Mr H:** With an extract: **paraphrase first**, in your own words. **Then** analyse.
**Mr H:** Jaques says a soldier goes seeking the bubble reputation, even in the cannon's mouth.
**Mei:** Point: Jaques **mocks** young soldiers who risk their lives for **fame**.
**Mei:** The metaphor '**bubble**' suggests fame is **shiny**, but **fragile** and **empty**, gone in an instant.
**Mei:** So ambition looks **hollow**. Not 'Shakespeare uses a metaphor'. What it **does**.
**Mr H:** That... is a very good paragraph.
**Narrator:** Before the bell, the English department would like to save you some marks.
**Mei:** Memory hooks. i-AM, five times: iambic pentameter. Thou, thee, thy, thine: like I, me, my, mine.
**Kevin:** One. **Wherefore** means **why**. Not where. Please. I'm begging.
**Nib:** Two. Shakespeare wrote **Early Modern English**. Not Old English.
**Mr H:** Three. Don't feature-spot. Explain what the technique **does**, and use **short, embedded** quotations.
**Will:** Four. Long speech to listeners: **monologue**. Alone on stage: **soliloquy**.
**Nib:** Five. **Thou** is not the posh one. It's **familiar**, or rude. **You** is polite.
**Will:** Six. I am the **earliest recorded user** of 'lonely'. Not, technically, its inventor. That hurt.
**Narrator:** Friday, 4 p.m. Mei submits her review.
**Mei:** Shakespeare: **four stars**.
**Will:** FOUR?
**Mei:** It was a bit long.
**Will:** Hamlet is four hours long!
**Mei:** Exactly.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** How many syllables are in a regular line of **iambic pentameter**?
**Mei:** **Ten**: five iambs, da-DUM, five times.
**Mr H:** What does **wherefore** mean?
**Kevin:** **Why**. Not where. Why.
**Mr H:** Who were the **groundlings**?
**Will:** The audience who paid **one penny** to **stand** in the **yard**.
**Mr H:** A character **alone on stage** speaks their private thoughts aloud. What is that called?
**Nib:** A **soliloquy**.
**Mr H:** Is **thou** the **polite** form, or the **familiar** one?
**Mei:** The **familiar** one. **You** is polite.
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Shakespeare's World & Language** quiz in your English Lab.
**Will:** Before you go. Five stars?
**Kevin:** I'd give him five.
**Will:** Thank you, Kevin.
